candidates.title: Shorten collection windows only where pickup timing supports it
candidates.proposal:
Upgrade source: “A clear collection deadline with checked daily release.” Preserve its private slips, phone-free identification, notification requirement, daily clearance and final status checks. Change the decision to shorten the window: the trial librarian first uses existing readiness and checkout timestamps to identify pickups that would have missed the proposed deadline. Inspect the branch calendar as well; a shorter window must preserve the minimum collection opportunity required by local policy, including closures. Historical timestamps indicate possible displacement, not how patrons would respond to a new deadline.

This mechanism frees shelf space through earlier clearance, but the added gate prevents adopting a shorter window merely because occupancy falls. Proceed only with policy authorization, reliable notification/deadline information and an explicitly accepted limit on displaced pickups. If those prerequisites are missing, enforce the existing window consistently. Preserve already promised deadlines and accessibility exceptions.

Print the exact deadline on private hold slips and communicate it through existing branch procedures, including paper during ordinary visits. Keep names and titles concealed; ordinary identification remains sufficient without a phone. Before release, match the physical item to its record, deadline, extensions and current status; check status again immediately before completing release. Leave uncertain items held for review. If interrupted, repeat verification before resuming rather than acting on an earlier check.

The librarian spends up to five extra minutes counting occupancy, ten checking releases and five reconciling pickups, errors and exceptions daily. Initial eligibility inspection uses this same allowance over several days. Compared with consistent clearance at the current deadline, any space benefit remains uncertain and must be weighed against lost collection opportunities and recovery work.
candidates.experiment: Run a three-week trial. First inspect available timestamps and upcoming closures within the daily allowance. If the prerequisite gate passes, alternate eligible newly ready holds between current and shorter windows using a predetermined rule; otherwise trial consistent clearance alone. Count occupied shelf positions at the same time daily. Use checkout timestamps to count actual pickups, distinguishing them from cancellations and releases. Log every detected mistaken release, including premature release, wrong-item release and missed extensions; audit every trial release against its entitlement. Record staff minutes and requests for recovery. Compare pickup rates and shelf-days after equal collection opportunities; report unfinished cohorts separately. Stop assigning shorter windows if the accepted displacement limit is exceeded, a closure invalidates the promised opportunity, or work exceeds 20 extra minutes daily. Honor existing trial promises and return new holds to the normal window. Three weeks may provide too few completed holds to justify adoption.

candidates.title: Offer staggered holds when patrons request several items
candidates.proposal:
Use a different mechanism: prevent unwanted simultaneous arrivals by letting patrons pace their unfilled requests during an ordinary, private counter interaction. Several previous routes accept the timing of ready holds as fixed. This route can work when patrons still want their books but cannot collect or use several arriving together.

The prerequisite is an existing circulation function that can suspend selected unfilled requests without an unintended loss of queue position, together with policy allowing staff to use it. The trial librarian verifies that behavior before enrollment. No new software is required. If the function or its consequences cannot be established, do not implement this route; retain ordinary holds and deadlines.

When a patron is already requesting multiple holds, offer to leave their chosen requests active and suspend others until a patron-selected date. Explain any known queue consequences privately. Participation is optional. Do not pause already ready or in-transit items, promise coordinated arrivals, or require an extra visit. The patron chooses dates during the current encounter, so resumption requires no new reminder or phone. Use automatic resumption only if supported; otherwise enroll only as many dated resumptions as the librarian can manage within the daily allowance.

Record consent, identifiers and resumption dates on staff-only printed slips. The librarian retains responsibility for manual resumptions until the circulation record confirms completion. Check due resumptions before enrolling anyone else; if interrupted or a resumption fails, preserve the slip for the next daily check and stop new enrollment until overdue actions are resolved. Normal identification supports phone-free pickup. Existing expiration release checks remain mandatory.

Allocate five extra minutes daily to offers and consent, five to due resumptions, and ten to measurement and release reconciliation. Compared with ordinary simultaneous requests, staggering could reduce abandoned ready holds, but it shifts cost into waiting and may merely postpone demand. It will have little value if simultaneous arrivals are uncommon.
candidates.experiment: Run for three weeks with a small enrollment cap that fits the daily allowance. Alternate comparable counter-service blocks between offering staggering and usual service; record offers, acceptance and selected requests privately. Count total shelf occupancy daily at a fixed time, and use existing timestamps to count actual pickups, ready-hold shelf-days and expired uncollected holds. Record mistaken releases separately and audit trial releases against identifiers, deadlines, extensions and current status. Also track suspended requests, overdue resumptions, staff minutes and patron requests to undo staggering. Stop enrollment after a missed resumption, an unexpected queue consequence or a daily workload over 20 minutes; resolve existing commitments before restarting. Compare abandonment and occupancy with usual-service blocks while reporting delayed requests explicitly. Inspect every outstanding resumption at trial end and retain responsibility until completed. Lower occupancy during the trial alone is insufficient: much of the apparent benefit could be deferred arrivals, requiring later timestamp inspection before a durable benefit can be claimed.
